chapters.title: Day 1: Number System - Factors, Multiples, HCF and LCM

body.text: A factor of a number divides it exactly, leaving no remainder. A multiple of a number is obtained by multiplying it by an integer.
HCF is the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly. It is found using prime factorization or the division method.

body.code:
HCF of 12 and 18:
12 = 2 x 2 x 3
18 = 2 x 3 x 3
HCF = 2 x 3 = 6

body.text: LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of two or more numbers.

rows: HCF x LCM = Number1 x Number2

body.code:
If HCF = 6 and LCM = 36, and one number is 12,
Other number = (6 x 36) / 12 = 18

body.text: HCF is always less than or equal to the smallest of the numbers; LCM is always greater than or equal to the largest.

items: Factors divide a number exactly; multiples are its products with integers.
HCF is the greatest common divisor; LCM is the smallest common multiple.
HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers (for exactly two numbers).
Prime factorization is the most reliable method for finding HCF and LCM.

chapters.title: Day 2: Simplification and BODMAS

body.text: BODMAS defines the order of operations to follow while solving a mathematical expression: Brackets, Orders (powers/roots), Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction.

body.code:
10 + 2 x (6 - 4) ÷ 2
Step 1 (Bracket): 10 + 2 x 2 ÷ 2
Step 2 (Division): 10 + 2 x 1
Step 3 (Multiplication): 10 + 2
Step 4 (Addition): 12

items: Solving addition before multiplication
Ignoring brackets and solving left to right
Mixing up division and multiplication order (they are done left to right, together)

body.text: Division and multiplication have equal priority and are solved left to right; the same applies to addition and subtraction.

items: BODMAS gives the correct order for solving mixed expressions.
Brackets are always solved first, followed by powers/roots.
Division and multiplication share priority and go left to right; same for addition and subtraction.
Careless order of operations is the most common source of simplification errors.

body.text: If a person can complete a piece of work in 'n' days, their one day's work is 1/n of the total work.

body.code:
A can finish a job in 10 days.
A's 1 day work = 1/10 of the total job

body.text: When two people work together, their individual daily work rates are added to find the combined rate.

body.code:
A finishes a job in 10 days, B finishes it in 15 days.
A's 1-day work = 1/10, B's 1-day work = 1/15
Combined 1-day work = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6
Together they finish the job in 6 days

body.text: 3. Finding Time When Only Some Days Are Worked Together

body.code:
A and B together do 1/6 of the work per day.
In 4 days, they complete: 4 x (1/6) = 4/6 = 2/3 of the work
Remaining work = 1/3

body.text: If a person is more 'efficient', they take fewer days; efficiency and time taken to complete work are inversely proportional.

body.code:

then A takes 20/2 = 10 days

body.text: Always convert 'days to finish' into 'work done per day' (as a fraction) before combining rates - this is the core trick of these problems.

items: A person's one-day work is 1 divided by the total days they need.

body.code:
Speed = Distance / Time
Distance = Speed x Time
Time = Distance / Speed

Convert 72 km/hr to m/s:

body.text: Always convert speed units to match the units used for time and distance before calculating - mismatched units are a common error source.
Average speed is NOT simply the average of two speeds - it depends on distance covered at each speed.

body.code:
If equal distances are covered at speeds a and b:
Average Speed = (2ab) / (a + b)

A travels at 40 km/hr and returns at 60 km/hr (same distance).
Average Speed = (2 x 40 x 60)/(40+60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/hr

A car covers 150 km in 3 hours. What is its speed?

items: Speed, distance, and time are related by Speed = Distance/Time.
Convert km/hr to m/s by multiplying by 5/18, and vice versa by 18/5.

chapters.title: Day 16: Problems on Trains (Rails)

concept.title: Time, Speed and Distance: Train Problems

body.text: Unlike simple speed problems, train problems must account for the length of the train itself, since the train must fully cross an object.

body.code: Time to cross a pole = Length of train / Speed of train

Train length = 150m, speed = 54 km/hr = 15 m/s
Time = 150/15 = 10 seconds

body.text: 3. Train Crossing a Platform or Bridge

body.code: Time to cross a platform = (Length of train + Length of platform) / Speed of train

Train length = 200m, platform = 100m, speed = 20 m/s
Time = (200+100)/20 = 15 seconds

Train A (100m, 20 m/s) and Train B (150m, 30 m/s), moving in opposite directions.
Relative speed = 20+30 = 50 m/s
Total length = 100+150 = 250m
Time to cross = 250/50 = 5 seconds

Train (150m, 20 m/s) crosses a man walking at 2 m/s in the SAME direction.
Relative speed = 20 - 2 = 18 m/s
Time = 150/18 ≈ 8.33 seconds

body.text: Always convert speeds to the same unit (usually m/s) before working with train length in meters and time in seconds.

items: Train problems always factor in the train's own length, unlike basic distance problems.
Time to cross a pole = train length / speed; crossing a platform adds the platform's length too.
When two trains move in opposite directions, use the sum of their speeds; same direction uses the difference.
A moving person crossed by a train is handled the same way, using relative speed.

rows: Speed of boat in still water

body.text: 3. Finding Boat and Stream Speed From Downstream/Upstream

body.code:
Boat Speed (b) = (Downstream + Upstream) / 2
Stream Speed (s) = (Downstream - Upstream) / 2

A boat's downstream speed is 16 km/hr, upstream speed is 8 km/hr.
Boat speed = (16+8)/2 = 12 km/hr
Stream speed = (16-8)/2 = 4 km/hr

A boat covers 24 km downstream in 2 hours.

body.text: Boats and streams problems use the exact same relative-speed logic as trains moving with or against each other.

items: Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed; upstream speed = boat speed - stream speed.
Boat speed = average of downstream and upstream speeds.

chapters.title: Day 18: Races and Relative Speed

body.text: In race problems, two or more runners cover a fixed distance, and the question usually asks about the head start (in distance or time) needed for a fair or given outcome.

body.code:
In a 100m race, A gives B a start of 10m.
This means when A runs 100m, B only needs to run 90m to finish together.

A gives B a start of 5 seconds in a race.
This means B starts running 5 seconds before A does.

A beats B by 20m in a 200m race.
This means when A finishes 200m, B has only covered 180m.

In a 100m race, A finishes in 10 seconds, B finishes in 12.5 seconds.
Speed of A = 100/10 = 10 m/s
Speed of B = 100/12.5 = 8 m/s
When A finishes (100m in 10s), B has covered: 8 x 10 = 80m
So A beats B by 100 - 80 = 20m

body.text: Race problems combine speed, time, and distance concepts directly - convert everything to speed first when comparing runners.

items: A 'start' given in distance means the other runner covers less total distance.
A 'start' given in time means the other runner begins running earlier.
'Beats by X meters' means the loser is X meters short when the winner finishes.
Converting race data into speed makes it easy to compare and solve these problems.

questions.explanation: Converting distance and time into speed makes race problems much easier to compare and solve.

chapters.title: Day 19: Averages - Basics

body.text: The average (or mean) of a set of numbers is the sum of all values divided by the count of values.

body.code: Average = Sum of all values / Number of values

Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four of them are 15, 18, 22, 25. Find the fifth.
Total = 20 x 5 = 100
Fifth number = 100 - (15+18+22+25) = 100 - 80 = 20

Average of 6 numbers is 30 (total 180).
A new number 44 is added.
New average = (180+44)/7 = 224/7 = 32

body.text: 5. Average Speed vs Average of Numbers
Remember: average speed for a journey with unequal times is different from a simple numeric average - use total distance / total time for those problems.

items: Average = total sum of values / number of values.
A missing value can be found once the average and count are known: Total = Average x Count.
Adding or removing a value changes both the total and the count, affecting the average.
True average speed problems require total distance divided by total time, not a simple average of speeds.

chapters.title: Day 20: Averages - Applications and Weighted Average

body.code:
Average of consecutive numbers from 1 to n = (n+1)/2
Average of 1 to 10 = (10+1)/2 = 5.5

Average age of 5 people is 24. A 6th person joins, new average becomes 25.
Old total = 24x5=120
New total = 25x6=150
Age of new person = 150-120 = 30

body.text: 3. Replacing a Value in the Group

body.code:
Average weight of 10 students is 40kg. One student weighing 30kg leaves,
and is replaced by one weighing 50kg. Find the new average.
Old total = 400
New total = 400 - 30 + 50 = 420
New average = 420/10 = 42kg

body.text: A weighted average accounts for groups of different sizes contributing to an overall average - larger groups count more.

body.code: Weighted Average = (n1 x a1 + n2 x a2) / (n1 + n2)

Class A: 30 students, average marks 70
Class B: 20 students, average marks 80
Overall average = (30x70 + 20x80)/(30+20) = (2100+1600)/50 = 3700/50 = 74

items: Consecutive number averages follow the simple formula (n+1)/2.
Age/replacement average problems are solved using total = average x count.
Replacing one value changes the total by (new value - old value).
Weighted average accounts for group sizes: larger groups pull the overall average more strongly toward their own average.

chapters.title: Day 21: Mixtures and Alligation

concept.title: Mixtures and the Rule of Alligation

body.text: Alligation is a technique used to find the ratio in which two ingredients at different prices (or concentrations) must be mixed to get a mixture at a desired price/concentration.

body.code: (Quantity of cheaper) / (Quantity of dearer) = (Price of dearer - Mean price) / (Mean price - Price of cheaper)

Tea at 40/kg mixed with tea at 60/kg to get a mixture worth 45/kg.
Ratio (cheaper:dearer) = (60-45) : (45-40) = 15:5 = 3:1

body.text: This means 3 parts of the 40/kg tea should be mixed with 1 part of the 60/kg tea.

body.code:
Milk solution A is 20% milk, solution B is 60% milk.
Mixed to get a solution that is 30% milk.
Ratio (A:B) = (60-30):(30-20) = 30:10 = 3:1

body.text: 5. Applying the Ratio to Find Actual Quantities

body.code:
If total mixture needed is 40 liters, and ratio is 3:1,
Quantity of A = (3/4) x 40 = 30 liters
Quantity of B = (1/4) x 40 = 10 liters

items: Alligation finds the mixing ratio between a cheaper/weaker and a dearer/stronger ingredient.
Ratio = (Dearer - Mean) : (Mean - Cheaper).
The same method works for prices, concentrations, or any two-value mixing problem.
Once the ratio is known, actual quantities are found by dividing the total using ratio parts.

chapters.title: Day 23: Partnership Problems

body.text: In a business partnership, profit is shared among partners based on how much capital they invested and for how long.

body.code:
If all partners invest for the same time period,
profit is shared purely in the ratio of their capital.
A invests 3000, B invests 5000. Profit = 1600.
Ratio = 3000:5000 = 3:5
A's share = (3/8)x1600=600, B's share=(5/8)x1600=1000

body.text: If partners invest for different durations, their share is based on (Capital x Time), not capital alone.

body.code:
A invests 4000 for 6 months, B invests 3000 for 8 months.
A's capital x time = 4000x6=24000
B's capital x time = 3000x8=24000
Ratio = 24000:24000 = 1:1 (equal share, despite different investments)

body.text: Always calculate Capital x Time for each partner first - this is the true basis of profit sharing, not capital alone.

items: Profit is shared based on each partner's investment and duration.
With equal time periods, profit is split purely by capital ratio.
With different time periods, profit is split by the ratio of Capital x Time.
Always compute Capital x Time for every partner before forming the sharing ratio.

body.text: Age problems are usually solved by assigning a variable to the present age and forming an equation based on the given past or future relationship.

body.code:

body.code:
5 years ago, A was twice as old as B. A is now 35.
A's age 5 years ago = 30
So B's age 5 years ago = 15

chapters.title: Day 25: Mean, Median and Mode

body.code:
Mean = Sum of all values / Number of values
Data: 4, 8, 6, 5, 3

body.text: The median is the middle value when data is arranged in order. For an even count of values, it is the average of the two middle values.

body.code:
Odd count: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 -> Median = 7 (middle value)
Even count: 2, 4, 6, 8 -> Median = (4+6)/2 = 5

body.text: Always arrange the data in ascending order before finding the median.
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set. A data set can have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all.

body.code:
Data: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6

rows: Data is categorical or has repeating values

Data: 10, 12, 13, 14, 100

Median = 13 (middle value)
Notice: the mean is skewed by the outlier 100, but median is not

Median is the middle value of ordered data; resistant to outliers.

chapters.title: Day 26: Range, Variance and Standard Deviation

concept.title: Measures of Spread: Range, Variance and Standard Deviation

body.text: Range is the simplest measure of spread - the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set.
2. Why We Need More Than Range
Range only looks at the two extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data is distributed - variance and standard deviation give a fuller picture.
Variance measures the average squared distance of each data point from the mean.

body.code:
Steps to calculate variance:
1. Find the mean
2. Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
3. Square each deviation
4. Find the average of the squared deviations

body.text: Standard Deviation is the square root of variance. It is expressed in the same unit as the original data, making it easier to interpret than variance.

body.code: SD = sqrt(Variance)

rows: Average squared distance from the mean
Typical distance from the mean, in original units

items: Range = Maximum value - Minimum value.
Variance is the average of squared deviations from the mean.
Standard Deviation is the square root of variance, and shares the original data's units.
A higher SD means data points are more spread out from the mean; a lower SD means they cluster closer to it.

questions.question: What is the formula for Range?
questions.explanation: Range is simply the difference between the maximum and minimum values.

questions.question: Find the range of the data set: 15, 22, 9, 30, 18.

questions.question: What does Variance measure?
options: The middle value of the data
The average squared distance from the mean
The total sum of the data
questions.explanation: Variance calculates the average of the squared deviations of each value from the mean.

questions.question: How is Standard Deviation related to Variance?
questions.explanation: Standard Deviation is calculated as the square root of the variance.

questions.question: Data: 1, 3, 5, 7. Mean = 4. What is the variance?
questions.explanation: Deviations: -3,-1,1,3; squared: 9,1,1,9; sum=20; variance=20/4=5.

concept.title: Data Interpretation: Bar Charts and Pie Charts

body.text: A bar chart represents data using rectangular bars, where the length or height of each bar shows the value it represents - useful for comparing categories.

body.text: A pie chart shows data as slices of a circle, where each slice's size represents its percentage share of the whole (which totals 100%).
4. Converting Pie Chart Percentages to Actual Values

body.code:

Actual sales of X = (30/100) x 5000 = 1500 units

chapters.title: Day 29: Permutations, Combinations and Probability Basics

concept.title: Introduction to Permutations, Combinations and Probability

body.text: A permutation counts the number of ways to arrange items where the order matters.

body.code:
nPr = n! / (n-r)!
Arranging 3 out of 5 people: 5P3 = 5!/(5-3)! = 5x4x3 = 60

body.text: A combination counts the number of ways to choose items where order does NOT matter.

body.code:
nCr = n! / (r! x (n-r)!)
Choosing 3 out of 5 people: 5C3 = 5!/(3! x 2!) = 10

body.text: Use permutations when arrangement/order matters (like a race finish order); use combinations when only the group selected matters (like a committee).

body.code: Probability = (Number of favorable outcomes) / (Total number of outcomes)

Probability of rolling a 4 on a fair die = 1/6
Probability of drawing a red card from a deck of 52 = 26/52 = 1/2
P(heads on a coin) x P(rolling a 6 on a die) = (1/2) x (1/6) = 1/12

items: Permutations count ordered arrangements: nPr = n!/(n-r)!.
Combinations count unordered selections: nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
Basic probability = favorable outcomes / total outcomes.
Independent combined events multiply their probabilities together.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a permutation and a combination?
options: Order matters in permutations but not in combinations
questions.explanation: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections.

questions.explanation: Even numbers (2,4,6) are 3 out of 6 outcomes, giving probability 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.question: For two independent events A and B, how is P(A and B) calculated?
questions.explanation: For independent events, the probability of both occurring is the product of their individual probabilities.

chapters.title: Day 30: Mini Project - Mixed Aptitude Test

concept.title: Final Mini Project: Applying Everything Together

body.text: This final day combines percentage, profit/loss, time and work, time-speed-distance, averages, and statistics into a set of mixed, real-world-style aptitude problems, just like an actual exam section.
2. Sample Combined Problem 1 - Percentage and Profit

body.code:
A shopkeeper marks an item 25% above cost price and gives a 10% discount.
CP = 800
MP = 800 x 1.25 = 1000
SP = 1000 x 0.9 = 900
Profit = 900 - 800 = 100
Profit% = (100/800) x 100 = 12.5%

body.text: 3. Sample Combined Problem 2 - Time, Speed and Work

body.code:
A can do a job in 12 days, B in 8 days.
Working together for 3 days, then A leaves.
Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/8 = 5/24 per day
Work done in 3 days = 3 x 5/24 = 15/24 = 5/8
Remaining work = 3/8, done by B alone at 1/8/day
Days needed by B = (3/8)/(1/8) = 3 days

Marks: 45, 60, 75, 80, 90
Mean = (45+60+75+80+90)/5 = 70
Median = 75 (middle value when sorted)
Range = 90 - 45 = 45

body.text: 5. Sample Combined Problem 4 - Trains and Averages

body.code:
A train 180m long crosses a platform 220m long in 20 seconds.
Speed = (180+220)/20 = 20 m/s = 72 km/hr

body.text: Real aptitude exams mix topics within a single question, so practicing combined problems like these builds true exam readiness.

Regular mixed practice, not just topic-by-topic practice, builds true exam speed and accuracy.
